summary:
Mission Control is a pixel-art web game where players design, launch and live through a complete crewed mission to the Moon or Mars. Players walk through an Earth headquarters where each room is one step of NASA's mission design process: set a science goal, choose a role, recruit an AI crew with real strengths and weaknesses, then design the mission on a shared planning board where every part, supply and rocket choice draws from the same mass, power and budget. After a go/no-go poll and launch, the mission plays out turn by turn in a habitat, where dust storms, equipment failures and discoveries test the plan. A debrief traces each outcome back to the decision that caused it, so players can redesign and try again. NOVA, an in-game robot guide, explains the real science just in time, from surviving long dark periods on batteries to life support and Mars signal delay.

The game answers the challenge by making mission trade-offs something players feel: improving one system always limits another. Built on NASA resources such as the Design and Develop Science Missions process, it helps students build systems thinking, teamwork and a clear understanding of why missions succeed or fail.
details:
What it does

Mission Control is a pixel-art strategy game played in the web browser. The player designs a complete crewed mission to the Moon or Mars, launches it, and then lives with the consequences of every decision.

How it works

1. Earth HQ: the player walks an astronaut (male or female) through a headquarters building. Each room is one step of NASA's mission design process: Mission Planning (destination and science goal), Personnel (choose a role and recruit crew), Briefing (design the mission) and Launch Control (verify and launch).

2. Team play in single player: the player picks one role (Science, Power & Life Support, Comms & Navigation, or Launch & Budget). AI teammates with their own strengths, weaknesses and priorities manage the other systems. Mass, power and budget come from one shared pool, so the player has to negotiate trades.

3. Design and verify: the player chooses parts, supplies and a launch vehicle, sees live resource margins, gets a list of mission requirements with how each is verified, and must pass a go/no-go poll before launch.

4. Fly the mission: in a Moon or Mars habitat, the mission runs turn by turn. Events based on real missions (dust storms, battery faults, solar flares, CO2 build-up, ice discoveries) require decisions about who acts and what it costs. What the player packed decides which fixes are possible. On Mars, signal delay means the crew sometimes follows standing orders without the player.

5. Debrief and retry: back on Earth, a debrief scores science, crew safety, efficiency and teamwork, and traces each problem back to the design decision that caused it. The player can redesign and fly again, comparing runs.

6. NOVA, an original robot guide, gives short lessons right when they are needed: predict first, explore an interactive visual, see the formula, then apply it to your own mission's numbers. Every lesson links its NASA source and is kept in a Codex.

Benefits and intended impact

Students usually learn orbits, power or rockets one topic at a time. Mission Control helps them understand a whole mission and how the pieces depend on each other. Players build systems thinking, learn real science, practise team decision-making, and learn from failure because the game explains why things went wrong. Three difficulty levels (Cadet, Engineer, Flight Director) and a sandbox make it suitable for beginners and space enthusiasts alike, and it runs in any modern browser with nothing to install.

Space agency resources

The game follows NASA's "Design and Develop Science Missions" process (six design steps and four mission segments: launch, space, ground and user). It also draws on the challenge resources, including the Mission Design Lab, Concept Maturity Levels and CubeSat 101. Moon and Mars values and crew life-support needs are based on NASA references, and events are inspired by real missions such as Apollo 13, Opportunity, Spirit and the ISS.

Tools and technologies

- Languages: TypeScript, HTML, CSS

- Frameworks and libraries: React, Vite, Phaser 3 (walkable isometric world), Tailwind CSS, Motion (animation), Zustand (game state and saves), Zod (content validation), Recharts (debrief charts), KaTeX (formulas), ZzFX and the Web Audio API (generated retro sound effects)

- Development: Git and GitHub, Vercel for hosting, Playwright for automated walkthroughs

- Hardware: laptops only

- AI tools (disclosed): Claude (Anthropic) via Claude Code helped write and test code; Gemini and ChatGPT helped create concept and pixel art, which the team edited. AI-generated images are labelled in the game.

How it is creative

Instead of menus and forms, the mission design process becomes a place you walk through. AI crewmates turn a single-player game into a team negotiation. The debrief turns failure into a cause-and-effect story instead of a game over, and the game connects every planning decision to what happens on the Moon or Mars.

What we considered

- Scientific accuracy vs. playability: real formulas and NASA-based values, simplified and clearly labelled as approximate where needed.

- Clarity for new players: a tutorial, just-in-time lessons and difficulty levels instead of long text.

- Scope: a reliable single-player experience with AI teammates, designed so real multiplayer can be added later.

- Accessibility: browser-based, keyboard controls, readable text and a reduced-motion option.

- Rules and originality: no NASA logos, original characters and art, and transparent disclosure of AI use.
